# What really happens when millions of Redis keys expire at once
### An experimental study of active expiration in Redis 7.2.17, 8.8.4 and 8.10.3

**Author:** Zeynalabdin ([@zeynallow](https://github.com/zeynallow))

*Technical report. All numbers are from `results/processed/` (regenerated by `analysis/analyze.py`
from the raw data in `results/raw/`). "Median [min–max]" unless stated otherwise. Detailed per-finding
evidence: `analysis/findings.md`. Source references: `analysis/source_code_notes.md`.*

---

## Abstract

Redis removes expired keys lazily (on access) and actively (a periodic, time-boxed sampling cycle).
We built Redis 7.2.17, 8.8.4 and 8.10.3 from source, added a research-only per-cycle trace to
`activeExpireCycle()`, and ran 588 valid experiment runs (plus 43 discarded runs, kept and documented): simultaneous and distributed mass
expiry, expiring keys mixed with long-TTL and with persistent keys, steady cache-like churn, client
load, forks, and large values.

Five results stand out:

1. **The active cycle's "10% stale" threshold behaves like a cliff that sits near 30–35%.** If ≤12%
   of the keys *with a TTL* are expired, Redis reclaims them at tens of keys per second. One pass
   over 1M keys takes about an hour, while the server is >99% idle. A binomial model of the stop
   rule predicts the measured rates of 8.8.4 within 0.9–1.15× from 5% to 40% expired. This follows
   from the code (a sequential scan cursor plus a per-batch stop rule) but is far from what the docs
   ("tests a few keys at random") suggest.
2. **Under steady churn, Redis ≤ 8.8.4 holds ~21% of TTL keys as expired garbage and oscillates.**
   8.10.3 holds ~9%. Rebuilding 8.10.3 with only the one-line fix of redis/redis#15412 reverted
   reproduces 8.8.4 to within ~1%, so that fix causes the difference: the FAST cycle's "too many
   stale keys" trigger was dead code from 6.0 to 8.8 (fraction vs percent). Adding 1M long-TTL
   keys multiplies the garbage by ~4.2× on both.
3. **A previously unreported stall.** After every mass expiry, active expiry examines *zero* keys
   while just under 1% of the expired keys remain. This lasts from 0.4 s (1M keys) to 6 s (8M),
   indefinitely with `activerehashing no`, and for the whole lifetime of a BGSAVE child. The cause is
   the "<1% filled → skip" rule measured against both hash tables of a dict that is mid-shrink. The
   plateau matches `1% × (old + new buckets)` to within a few keys at 1M–8M keys. A one-condition
   patch removes it with no measurable CPU cost (reported upstream as redis/redis#16111; write-up: `reports/upstream_issue.md`).
4. **Tail latency during mass expiry is set by `hz`, not by `active-expire-effort`.** Default: p99
   ~27 ms while 1M keys expire (vs ~1 ms otherwise). Effort 10: ~50 ms and no faster under load.
   `hz 100`: 5–8 ms and faster cleanup.
5. **Client traffic roughly doubles expiry throughput** (FAST cycles run once per event-loop
   iteration). Large composite values freed synchronously overrun the 1 ms FAST budget by up to
   48×; `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` fixes that.

We also document the measurement pitfalls we hit: host-speed drift on the VM (up to 1.5×, which
produced two wrong preliminary conclusions that a round-robin re-test retracted), a load generator
that saturated its own connections, a design error (listpack-encoded "big" hashes), and a
monitoring observer effect (100 Hz `INFO` polling speeds expiry up by ~30%).

---

## 1. Background

**Two expiration paths** (N1). *Passive*: every key lookup calls `expireIfNeeded()` (`db.c:2999`),
which deletes the key on a master. *Active*: `activeExpireCycle()` (`expire.c:287`) runs as a
**SLOW** cycle from `serverCron` (`hz` times/s; budget 25% of the cron period, i.e. 25 ms at
`hz 10`) and as a **FAST** cycle (budget 1 ms) from `beforeSleep()`, i.e. potentially on every
event-loop iteration, rate-limited to one per 2 ms. FAST cycles start only if the previous cycle hit
its time limit or the estimated stale share is high (N5).

**Sampling** (N3, N4). Since 6.0 (commit `ffc7e509a`) the cycle walks the `expires` hash table with a
persistent `SCAN`-style cursor, in batches of `20 + 5·(effort−1)` keys. After each batch it repeats
only if more than `10 − (effort−1)` percent of the batch was expired. Otherwise it moves to the next
database.

**`active-expire-effort`** (1–10, N2) scales batch size, FAST budget, SLOW CPU share (25%→43%) and
the stale threshold (10%→1%).

**Memory.** `used_memory` drops when a key is freed. RSS drops only when jemalloc purges dirty pages
(N10).

## 2. Research questions

| ID | Hypothesis |
|---|---|
| H1 | Simultaneous expiry of many keys delays reclamation by seconds. |
| H2 | Higher `active-expire-effort` is not uniformly better (faster cleanup vs latency/CPU). |
| H3 | Simultaneous, uniform and concentrated expiry schedules behave differently. |
| H4 | Redis can hold substantial memory in expired-but-present keys; metrics do not show it clearly. |
| H5 | Under client load, active expiry competes with request processing. |
| H6 | Further edge cases suggested by the code (refined during the study into H6a–f; see `analysis/hypotheses.md`). |

## Methodology (summary of what was run and how)

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Machine | KVM guest, Intel Xeon @ 2.80 GHz (Cascade Lake family, model 85), 4 vCPU, 1 thread/core |
| Memory | 15.7 GiB, **no swap** (verified before/after every run: `swap_used_kb = 0`) |
| OS | Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, kernel 6.18.44 (Firecracker-style VM) |
| Compiler | gcc 13.3.0, Redis default flags (`-O3 -flto -fno-omit-frame-pointer`), `MALLOC=jemalloc` (bundled jemalloc 5.3.0) |
| THP | `madvise` |
| `vm.overcommit_memory` | 1 (set for the fork experiments, as Redis recommends) |
| Tools | Python 3.13 + redis-py 8.1/hiredis, numpy, matplotlib; perf 6.8; custom C load generator |

This is a single, virtualized machine. Absolute numbers (keys/s, ms) are specific to it. The ratios and
mechanisms are what we generalize, and only where the source code explains them.

### Isolation and controls

* **Fresh process per run.** Every measurement starts a new `redis-server` (clean allocator, empty
  dicts) with `environment/redis.conf`, plus explicit overrides recorded with `CONFIG GET *` in the raw
  file. Persistence is off (`save ""`, `appendonly no`) except in the fork experiment.
* **CPU pinning.** `redis-server` on CPU 1, harness/poller on CPU 0, load generator on CPUs 2-3.
* **Server-side loading.** Keys are created by Lua `EVAL` batches (20k keys/batch) with an absolute
  `PXAT`, so the logical expiry instant `T` is known to the millisecond and the client cannot be a
  loading bottleneck. A run is discarded automatically if loading did not finish ≥0.5 s before `T`, or
  if any key expired early.
* **Separation of phases.** Load, then idle until `T` (load-induced rehashing completes), then measure.
* **Clocks.** `time.monotonic()` for durations. Wall clock only to align with `PXAT`. The trace uses the
  server's `ustime()`, which is the same clock as `PXAT`.
* **Measuring without perturbing.** The poller uses only `INFO` (memory, stats, keyspace, cpu,
  persistence), `DBSIZE` and `/proc/<pid>`. None of these look up individual keys, so they never trigger
  passive expiration. They do wake the event loop, and that effect is quantified (F4). Default poll
  interval: 200 ms (1 s for long runs).
* **Ground truth for "expired but present".** For every scenario the full expiry schedule is known, so
  `stale(t) = physically present keys − keys whose PXAT > t`. Physically present keys come from DBSIZE
  (unmodified builds) or, at cycle resolution, from the trace (`expires_left` after each cycle).
* **Repetitions.** 3–5 per configuration. Summaries report the median with min–max. Every run is kept in
  `results/raw/` (one gzip'd JSON file, plus the per-cycle trace and per-request latency log where
  applicable).

### Instrumentation (research-only builds)

`instrumentation/apply_expire_trace.py` adds, to a copy of each version, a per-cycle record written
at the end of `activeExpireCycle()`: start time, elapsed µs, type (slow/fast), whether the time limit
was hit, iterations, keys sampled, keys expired, and keys left in `db->expires`. Rejected FAST attempts
are counted as well. The buffer is `mmap`ed, outside jemalloc, so `used_memory` is unaffected. It costs
one `ustime()`-free struct write per cycle. Instrumented builds are named `*-trace` and every table
says which build produced it. Latency numbers come only from unmodified builds.

`8.10.3-revert15412-trace` is 8.10.3 with only the one-line #15412 fix reverted. It isolates that change
from everything else that differs between 8.8.4 and 8.10.3.

### Load generator

`tools/loadgen.c`: N threads, one blocking hiredis connection each, open-loop schedule (fixed rate per
thread). Latency is measured from the **scheduled** send time, which avoids coordinated omission. Every
request is logged. A first version (2 connections × 5000 req/s) was discarded: each connection was
~75% busy at baseline, so any server slowdown caused client-side queueing of hundreds of ms that
said more about the client than about Redis. The raw data is kept in `results/raw/_discarded/`. The
final setup uses 8 connections × 1250 req/s (10k req/s total).

### Environment epochs and quarantined runs

The cloud container was restarted several times during the study. One restart moved the session to a
different kernel build (`6.18.44-fc-v180` → `6.18.44-fc-v185`), and the identical reference
configuration became ~30% faster there (sentinel suite: 1.03–1.26 µs per expired key vs 1.40–1.56
before). Every raw file records the kernel. Rules applied:

* **Each suite is homogeneous**: all of its runs come from one environment. Comparisons are made only
  within a suite, or between suites from the same environment.
* Suites recorded on v180: `latency`, `latency_trace`, `churn`, `effort`, `distribution`, `persist`,
  `observer`, `cliff_versions`, `bytes`, `cliff_epoch_v180`. All others ran on v185. Absolute
  times differ across the two; the mechanisms and ratios reported were checked within one environment.
* `cliff_epoch_v180` (24 runs) was kept and the whole `cliff` suite was re-run on v185. This doubles as
  a cross-machine robustness check.
* Quarantined, kept in `results/raw/_discarded/` with a README each, excluded from analysis:
  1. `latency_v1_per_connection_saturated`: flawed load-generator design (see above);
  2. `contaminated_by_concurrent_build`: 34 files recorded while I compiled a Redis build on another
     core. Those runs were 1.4–1.6× slower than identical runs, so after that no other work ran
     alongside an experiment;
  3. `fork_epoch_v180_partial`: 5 fork runs from before the environment change;
  4. `bigvalues_listpack_design_error`: 500-field hashes are listpack-encoded under the default
     `hash-max-listpack-entries 512`, so they did not test large composite values.


## 3. Source code analysis (summary)

Full notes with line numbers and commits: `analysis/source_code_notes.md`. The points that explain
the results:

| # | Code | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| N3 | `expire.c:425-438`: `kvstoreScan(db->expires, db->expires_cursor, ...)`, persistent cursor | A deterministic sweep, not random sampling. The stale share ahead of the cursor stays constant until it wraps. |
| N4 | `expire.c:447`: `repeat = ... expired*100/sampled > config_cycle_acceptable_stale` | ≤10% stale → one ~20-key batch per DB per cycle. |
| N5 | `expire.c:323-325`: FAST gate. 8.10.0+: `stale_perc * 100 < acceptable_stale`; ≤8.8.4: no `* 100` | Before 8.10 the stale trigger never fires (#15412). |
| N2 | `expire.c:347`: `timelimit = slow_perc * 1e6 / hz / 100` | The SLOW slice is 25 ms at hz 10, 2.5 ms at hz 100. |
| N6 | `expire.c:482`: time checked every 16 iterations | Expensive deletions overrun the budget. |
| N7 | `ae.c:338-340`: next timer = end of callback + period | The 25% budget is effectively ~20% (cron period 126 ms vs 100 ms). |
| N8/N11 | `expire.c:130-145` skip if `numkeys*100/dictBuckets < 1`; `dict.h:229` `dictBuckets = ht[0]+ht[1]`; rehash advanced only by cron (`server.c:1331-1361`, `kvstore.c:674`) | Stall at ~1% during a shrink, indefinitely without cron rehash or during a fork. |

## 4. Experimental results

### 4.1 H1 – Simultaneous expiry

`core` suite (v185, unmodified builds, idle, versions interleaved per round; stopped early at 61/108
runs, n = 1–2 per cell; `charts/core_reclaim_time.png`):

| keys × value | time to remove all (7.2.17 / 8.8.4 / 8.10.3) | used_memory loaded → after | RSS loaded → 12 s after → after `MEMORY PURGE` (8.10.3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10k × 64 B | 0.4 / 0.4 / 0.3 s | 3 MiB → 1.4 MiB | 11 → 10 → 10 MiB |
| 100k × 64 B | 1.1 / 1.0 / 0.7 s | 17 MiB → 1.7 MiB | 27 → 23 → 19 MiB |
| 500k × 64 B | 4.7 / 3.7 / 4.1 s | 72 MiB → 1.8 MiB | 87 → 43 → 30 MiB |
| 1M × 64 B | 8.8 / 8.4 / 7.8 s | 143 MiB → 1.7 MiB | 155 → **87** → 32 MiB |
| 1M × 1 KB | 11.8 / 9.6 / 9.2 s | 1,287 MiB → 1.7 MiB | 1,308 → 33 → 29 MiB |
| 1M × 4 KB | – / 13.0 / 14.0 s | 4,950 MiB → 1.7 MiB | 5,004 → 61 → 58 MiB |


**Answer to H1:** yes. Reclamation is spread over seconds and grows linearly with the number of
keys, at ~110–135k keys/s idle for small values. The SLOW cycle is capped at 25 ms per (stretched)
cron tick, so the expiry duty is ~20% of one core and an idle server takes ~5× longer than the raw
deletion work. A ~1% tail is additionally delayed by the rehash stall (F5).

### 4.2 H3 – Expiry distribution

`distribution` suite (v180, 1M × 64 B, idle, 5 reps; trace builds; `charts/distribution.png`). A = all at T;
B = uniform over 10 s; C = normal(T+5 s, σ = 0.5 s).

| | peak expired-but-present keys | mean over 0–12 s | last key removed (after T) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (7.2.17 / 8.8.4 / 8.10.3) | 989k / 983k / 987k | 418k / 386k / 345k | 9.1 / 7.8 / 7.8 s |
| B | 443k / 436k / 446k | 348k / 310k / 354k | 14.6 / 13.3 / 14.5 s |
| C | 863k / 849k / 871k | 419k / 392k / 446k | 14.0 / 13.0 / 14.3 s |

Spreading expiry over 10 s lowers the *peak* garbage by ~55%, but not the *average*. The cursor
passes over keys that will expire a moment later, and those then wait for the next sweep. The last
key disappears ~3–5 s after the last logical expiry in every schedule. 5 reps per cell (the 8.10.3 B-r4/C runs
were re-run after the first attempt was quarantined, see Methodology).

### 4.3 H6a – The stale-share cliff (expired keys among long-TTL keys)

See `analysis/findings.md` F1 for the full table and `charts/cliff.png`. In short (v185, 3 reps per
point, 1M TTL keys):

| expiring share | 8.8.4 removed after 60 s | 8.10.3 removed after 60 s | model rate | measured 8.8.4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5% | 1.3% | 1.3% | 11 /s | 11 /s |
| 10% | 1.8% | 1.9% | 30 /s | 31 /s |
| 20% | 6.3% | 12.7% | 194 /s | 209 /s |
| 30% | 38.5% | 72.2% | 1,691 /s | 1,932 /s |
| 35% | 100% (54 s) | 100% (36 s) | – | – |
| 50% | 100% (5.3 s) | 100% (5.4 s) | – | – |

With *persistent* instead of long-TTL neighbours, 10% expiring keys vanish in ~1 s (`persist`). With
10% expired, one full cursor pass over 100k TTL keys takes 326 s (predicted ~320 s, `sweep`). A
client-side `SCAN` clears 100k stale keys among 1M in 1.1–3.0 s (`mitigation`).

### 4.4 H4 – Hidden memory

* `bytes` (v180): 1M live 64-byte keys + 100k expired 4 KB keys. After 2 minutes, 96.7–96.9% of the
  expired keys are still present and `used_memory` is 632 MiB (8.10.3) / 666 MiB (7.2.17).
  `expired_stale_perc` reads 7–9%. The sampler counts keys, not bytes, so the expired values are a
  large majority of `used_memory` while the stale *share* looks healthy.
* `churn_long` (v185): with 5k expirations/s and 1M long-TTL keys, 8.8.4 holds ~346k expired keys
  (peaking at 561k) and 8.10.3 ~132k.
* Nothing in INFO reports expired-but-present keys directly. `keys=` / `DBSIZE` include them, and
  `expired_stale_perc` is an estimate of their share *of TTL keys*. In our runs it tracked the true
  share reasonably (e.g. 7–9% estimated vs 9–10% true in `cliff`/`bytes`; ~14% vs 9.2% in 8.10.3
  churn, ~32% vs 21% pre-fix churn). It overestimates under churn, because sampling stops right after
  batches rich in expired keys.
* Allocator retention (`core`): `used_memory` returns to baseline as keys are deleted. RSS returns
  quickly for large values (5 GB → 61 MiB in 12 s) but lags for many small ones (1M × 64 B: 18–87 MiB
  RSS vs ~1.5 MiB used after 12 s; 18–32 MiB after `MEMORY PURGE`). That is allocator retention,
  distinct from expired-but-present keys, and visible in `allocator_resident` vs `allocator_allocated`.

### 4.5 H2 / H5 – Effort, hz and latency under load

`latency` suite (v180, unmodified builds, 10k GET/s open-loop over 8 connections, 1M keys expiring,
5 reps; `charts/latency_scatter.png`):

| config (all 3 versions behave alike) | p99 during expiry | max | expiry finished |
|---|---|---|---|
| no expiry (baseline) | 0.5–0.9 ms | 5–7 ms | – |
| effort 1, hz 10 (default) | 26.3–27.1 ms | 29.6–31.3 ms | 3.5 s |
| effort 10, hz 10 | 49.8–50.4 ms | 53.9–57.3 ms | 3.0–3.5 s |
| effort 1, hz 100 | 5.4–8.5 ms | 9.4–14.9 ms | 2.0 s |

Under load the cycle trace (`latency_trace`) shows FAST cycles at ~230/s doing 67–69% of the
deletions, and an expire duty cycle of ~40% (vs ~20% idle). 1M keys clear in ~3.1 s instead of
7.5 s. Idle (`effort`, `interleave`): higher effort clears faster (8.10.3: 7.5 s → 4.8 s from effort
1 to 10, confirmed monotonic by the round-robin re-test) but stretches the longest cycle from ~26 to
~47 ms. Total expire CPU is unchanged (~1.5 s per 1M keys).

**Answer to H2:** no, higher effort is not uniformly better. It compresses the same CPU work into
longer stalls. Under load it doubled p99 without finishing sooner. `hz` controls the slice length,
and raising it improved both the tail and the cleanup time here, at the cost of a higher median.

**Answer to H5:** yes, in both directions. Expiry takes up to ~40% of the main thread under load,
and the load makes expiry run ~2× faster (more FAST cycles).

### 4.6 Further edge cases (H6)

* **Steady churn (H6e, #15412):** F2. 8.8.4 ≈ 21% of TTL keys stale and oscillating with a
  ~150 s period (`charts/churn_long.png`); 8.10.3 ≈ 9% and flat. Causality shown with the
  single-line revert build.
* **Rehash stall (H6f):** F5. Exact plateau prediction at 1M–8M keys. Never ends without cron
  rehashing. A one-line patch removes it.
* **Fork (H6b):** F8. Active expiry stops at ~10.5k keys (≈1% of the table) for the entire
  ~95 s BGSAVE on all versions. The child's copy-on-write pins ~1.1 GB, parent+child footprint
  +6–9%.
* **Large values (H6c):** F6. 1,000-field hashes freed synchronously: SLOW cycles 49–77 ms (budget
  25 ms), FAST cycles up to 48.6 ms (budget 1 ms). `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` → ~25 ms and 10–15×
  faster cleanup.
* **Observer effect (H6d):** 100 Hz `INFO` polling: 7.65 s → 5.24 s (8.10.3). 5 Hz: no effect.
* **CPU per key (F9):** 7.2.17 spends 1.17× [1.09–1.27] the CPU per expired key of 8.10.3 (paired,
  round-robin).

### 4.7 Where the CPU goes

**Profile** (`profile`, perf at 1999 Hz during the expiry window, 1M × 64 B, unmodified builds, LTO, so
inlined symbols are attributed approximately; `results/processed/profile_*.txt`). The expire cycle
splits roughly into **finding the keys**: walking buckets and touching each entry, ~30–38%
(`activeExpireCycle`/`expireScanCallback` + `dictScanDefragBucket`), mostly cache misses on
dict entries. Then **deleting**: `dbGenericDelete` → `dictTwoPhaseUnlinkFind` re-hashes the key and
searches the main keyspace dict, ~10%. Then **freeing**: `sdsfree`/`zfree`/`je_malloc_usable_size`/tcache
flushes, ~15–30%. Hashing (`siphash`) is ~1%. No single hotspot dominates. The cost per key is mostly
memory access, which fits the ~1.5–2 µs per key and its sensitivity to host noise.

## 5. Unexpected findings

1. **The cliff is at ~30–35%, not 10%** (F1). We expected expiry to slow down below 10% stale. We
   did not expect it to be ~3,000× slower at 10% than at 50% (31 vs ~94,000 keys/s), or that 30% stale would still leave a
   majority of the garbage after a minute on 8.8.4.
2. **Long-TTL neighbours, not persistent keys, cause the garbage**, and the garbage scales with them
   (F1, F2).
3. **Pre-8.10 Redis oscillates under steady churn** (F2): a relaxation oscillation with a ~150 s
   period and garbage peaking at 1.6× its median.
4. **The 1% skip rule stalls expiry during dict shrinks and forks** (F5, F8), with plateau values
   predicted exactly by bucket arithmetic.
5. **Traffic speeds expiry up; effort can make latency worse without speeding it up** (F3, F4).
6. **Methodological surprises:** VM host drift of up to 1.5× in per-key cost within an hour, which
   made two preliminary conclusions wrong (F9); and the observer effect of monitoring.

## 6. Root cause analysis

* F1/F2 follow from N3 + N4: a sequential cursor plus a per-batch stop rule at >10%. With p ≤ 10%,
  P(≥3 of 20 expired) ≤ 0.32, so each cycle examines ~20–30 keys per DB. The binomial model
  `10 × 20/(1−q(p)) × p` matches 8.8.4 within 0.9–1.15× over 5–40% stale (`charts/cliff.png`).
  This is **design behaviour**: commit `276680568` (2019) deliberately lowered the tolerance from 25%
  to 10%. The same commit introduced the FAST-cycle stale gate whose unit mismatch was fixed in #15412. What is undocumented is its magnitude and its dependence on long-TTL keys.
* The pre-8.10 oscillation is the same rule plus the missing FAST trigger (N5). The trigger was
  intended (comment and code since 6.0) but disabled by a unit mismatch. It was fixed upstream in
  #15412 (8.10.0). Our revert build shows this fix alone explains the difference. This was a
  **defect, already fixed**.
* F5/F8 follow from N11: the skip rule's "the dictionary will be resized asap" assumption fails when
  the resize is in progress, because `dictBuckets()` counts both tables, nothing on the expire path
  advances the rehash, and cron rehashing is time-sliced (keys dict first), optional
  (`activerehashing`), and disabled during forks. This is a **likely defect** (unintended
  interaction). Patch and evaluation: `reports/upstream_issue.md`.
* F3/F6 follow from N2 and N6: slice length = budget × cron period, and budget enforcement is
  coarse-grained. **Design behaviour**, worth documenting.
* F4 follows from N1/N5: FAST cycles are tied to event-loop iterations. **Design behaviour.**

## 7. Limitations

* **One virtual machine**, 4 vCPU. Absolute times and rates are machine-specific and drifted up to
  1.5× over the study. We report within-suite comparisons, use round-robin ordering for CPU-cost
  claims, and rely on mechanisms that the source code explains.
* **Two environments.** A container restart moved the study to a different kernel/host, where the
  reference configuration became ~30% faster. Each suite was kept within one environment.
* **Latency** was measured only in the first environment. The second host had sporadic ~150 ms VM
  pauses that made client-side latency unreliable, so no latency claims are made from it.
* **Standalone mode only.** Cluster mode (one dict per slot, `kvstore` skips) and replicas (which
  never actively expire) were not tested. The stale-share mechanics are per dict and would apply per
  slot in cluster mode, which we did not verify.
* **Instrumented builds** add one record per cycle. They were used for cycle-level timing. Latency
  and the core matrix use unmodified builds.
* **Key/value shapes**: mostly short string keys with 64 B–4 KB values plus one large-hash
  experiment. Other types, module types and hash-field expiry (Redis 8) were not studied.
* **Repetitions** are 2–6 per configuration. Ranges are reported. Where they overlap, we do not
  claim a difference.
* Prior-report search: a web search and the redis/redis git history. The GitHub issue tracker
  itself was not searched, so F5 may already be known.

## 8. Practical implications

1. **Run Redis ≥ 8.10 for TTL-heavy caches.** Under churn it holds ~2.6× fewer expired keys and does
   not oscillate (F2).
2. **The denominator is keys-with-TTL.** Mixing very long and very short TTLs in one database lets
   short-TTL garbage pile up (F1, F2). Persistent keys don't have this effect. Separating TTL classes
   (database/instance), or using `active-expire-effort` (whose 1% threshold removes the cliff at
   higher CPU and stall cost), are the levers.
3. **Watch `expired_stale_perc`.** Persistently >10% means a material share of TTL keys is garbage.
   It counts keys, not bytes: if expired values are large, memory can be dominated by garbage while
   the gauge shows ~8% (F1 "bytes").
4. **For latency, tune `hz` first.** At hz 10, a mass expiry adds ~25 ms stalls. `active-expire-effort`
   lengthens them (F3).
5. **Turn on `lazyfree-lazy-expire` if values are large collections** (F6).
6. **Don't expect expiry to free memory during BGSAVE/AOF rewrite.** Expiry stops at ~1% and
   copy-on-write grows (F8).
7. **A periodic `SCAN`** is a cheap, effective sweeper on a master (F1 "mitigation").
8. **Spread TTLs (jitter)** to cut the peak, not the average, of expired-but-present keys (H3).
9. **When benchmarking Redis on VMs**, interleave configurations. Block-ordered comparisons can be
   wrong by 20%+ (F9).

## 9. Conclusion

What we demonstrated, on one machine with three Redis versions:

* Active expiration is a **deterministic cursor sweep governed by a per-batch stop rule**, not random
  sampling. Its reclamation rate depends steeply on the share of expired keys among *keys with a
  TTL*. The rate is ~30 keys/s at 10% and ~94k keys/s at 50%, and a simple binomial model predicts it
  (F1).
* As a result, **Redis tolerates far more garbage than "10%" suggests**. Up to 8.8.4 it held ~21% of
  TTL keys under steady churn, in a slow oscillation. 8.10.3 holds ~9%, and we showed the one-line
  #15412 fix is the cause (F2).
* We found **a stall in the active cycle** caused by the "<1% fill" skip rule during dict shrinks
  and forks, predicted it to within a few keys, and wrote and evaluated a one-condition fix (F5, F8).
  Reported upstream as [redis/redis#16111](https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/16111); write-up in `reports/upstream_issue.md`.
* For latency, **`hz` sets the stall length during mass expiry, and `active-expire-effort` makes it
  worse** (F3). Traffic itself accelerates expiry (F4). Large values need `lazyfree-lazy-expire`
  (F6).

We did **not** demonstrate anything about cluster mode, replicas, or other hardware. The absolute
numbers are specific to this VM. The mechanisms are tied to specific lines of code and were
reproduced across versions and two host environments. Two preliminary conclusions (a version
difference in per-key cost and a non-monotonic effort effect) were artefacts of host drift, and
were retracted after a round-robin re-test. We report them so the method can be judged.
